candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XVI.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I will rain bread from heaven for you' — the manna of the wilderness is for Ephrem the direct prophetic anchor of Jn 6: 'I am the bread which came down from heaven.' The wilderness bread sustains the body for a day; the Eucharist sustains the soul for eternity. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Ex 16:4 and Jn 6 together as the OT-NT diptych of the eucharistic gift.
candidates.reviewer_notes: Curated PD interpretive summary representing the Ethiopian Tewahedo tradition's reading via Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus. Verify the summary still reflects the source's argument before promoting; substitute a verbatim quote from the NPNF / Charles dump where available, and where applicable cross-check the Andəmta homiletic tradition for resonance.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus XVI.6 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When Israel sees the manna they say 'man hu' — 'what is it?' — and the question itself becomes the name. Ephrem hears in this the canonical instinct that the heavenly food cannot be named by its likeness to anything earthly; the name is a confession of mystery. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites this as the OT antecedent of its own anaphoral language of 'mystery,' 'gift,' and 'medicine of life.'

candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When Israel sees the manna they say 'man hu' — 'what is it?' — and the question itself becomes the name. Ephrem hears in this the canonical instinct that the heavenly food cannot be named by its likeness to anything earthly; the name is a confession of mystery. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites this as the OT antecedent of its own anaphoral language of 'mystery,' 'gift,' and 'medicine of life.'
